Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 7 CHAPTER 2 Modeling and Machine Learning Primer 2.1 The Modern Process Engineer's Evolving Toolkit For process engineers, the core expertise lies in understanding, predicting, and controlling complex water systems through the application of mostly mechanistic models. This chapter builds upon that foundation, introducing ML not as a replacement for fundamental engineering principles, but as a powerful and necessary extension of the modern analytical toolkit. It frames the adoption of data-driven methods as a logical evolution in process modeling, catalyzed by a revolution in data availability and computational power. The objective is to provide a conceptual framework that equips users to identify opportunities for ML, understand its core paradigms, and engage critically with its application in the WRRF environment. 2.1.1 The Bedrock: Mechanistic Models The practice of process engineering is built upon the bedrock of mechanistic modeling. These models, which are constructed from the fundamental principles of physics, chemistry, and biology, provide a causal understanding of system behavior. A prime example from the wastewater sector is the family of Activated Sludge Models (ASMs) (e.g., Henze et al. 2000). The hybrid model developed for biological nutrient removal control in this report’s second case study (Application 2) incorporates such a component, demonstrating the continued relevance of these foundational tools. The strength of mechanistic models lies in their deductive capability; because they are based on causal mechanisms, they can, once validated, be used to extrapolate and predict system behaviors not explicitly present in the original calibration data (Baker et al. 2018). However, the power of mechanistic models is accompanied by significant practical limitations. A core challenge is that these models are, by necessity, a simplification of reality, which results in structural uncertainty and a constant need for calibration (Duarte et al. 2023. Sin and Al 2021). This calibration process can be exceptionally complex, time-consuming, and costly, often requiring intensive measurement campaigns to estimate the dozens of parameters involved (Sin and Al 2021). Furthermore, established frameworks can be inflexible. Such limitations were evident even in this project; for example, in the carbon diversion case study (Application 1), the report notes that traditional mechanistic modeling approaches were found to be "inadequate for robust prediction of dynamic behavior" in the high-rate contact stabilization (HR-CS) system. It is precisely these gaps—in handling complexity, integrating diverse data, and adapting to dynamic conditions—that have created the imperative for new modeling paradigms. This evolution represents more than a simple change in tools; it signifies a fundamental shift in the epistemological approach to process control. Mechanistic models are driven by a quest for causal understanding—a desire to answer the question, "Why does this system behave this way?" (Baker et al. 2018).
